results.finding: HE is defined by the West Haven criteria (grades 0-IV). Diagnosis requires evidence of liver disease, neuropsychiatric disturbance, and exclusion of other causes. Ammonia correlates poorly with grade. Neuroimaging is required to exclude structural causes including intracranial hemorrhage, particularly in cirrhotics with coagulopathy. Precipitant identification and treatment is the cornerstone of management.
results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease: 2014 Practice Guideline by AASLD and EASL

results.finding: Infection is among the most common precipitants of overt HE. Urinary tract infection should be screened for in all cirrhotics presenting with AMS. Lactulose and rifaximin remain first-line. Incomplete response to lactulose mandates re-evaluation for concurrent structural pathology, particularly in coagulopathic patients with a history of falls.
results.title: The modern management of hepatic encephalopathy

results.finding: A focal neurological deficit or failure of expected clinical improvement on standard HE therapy should prompt urgent neuroimaging to exclude structural lesions. Cirrhotic coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia confer significantly elevated risk for intracranial hemorrhage, including chronic subdural collections, particularly after even minor head trauma.
results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy

output.summary: AASLD/EASL guidelines require exclusion of alternate structural causes in HE by neuroimaging. Focal neurological signs or incomplete response to standard therapy should prompt re-evaluation for structural pathology. Cirrhotic coagulopathy markedly increases risk for subdural collections, even after trivial falls. Infection is a leading HE precipitant. Management hierarchy: identify and treat precipitant, initiate lactulose/rifaximin, repeat neuroimaging if clinically atypical.

alternatives: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg extended-release BID x 5 days if E. coli susceptible and eGFR adequate
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as alternative if oral route unreliable
Acetaminophen 500 mg q6h (max 2 g/day in liver disease) for headache analgesia — safer than opioids or NSAIDs
contraindications: Benzodiazepines: contraindicated in overt HE — precipitate and prolong encephalopathy via GABA-A potentiation; avoid for agitation or sleep
Opioid analgesics (morphine, oxycodone): contraindicated in HE — impaired hepatic clearance, CNS depression; use paracetamol (acetaminophen) at hepatic-safe dose if analgesia required
Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC): avoid initiation given coagulopathy (INR 1.8) and chronic subdural hematoma without neurosurgical clearance
NSAIDs: avoid — risk of GI hemorrhage, renal impairment in cirrhosis

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute all AMS to HE and forego neuroimaging — focal right-sided signs (pronator drift, hyperreflexia) and unilateral headache are not explained by HE alone and mandate CT head to exclude structural pathology.

Do not be falsely reassured by partial lactulose improvement — incomplete recovery with persistent focal deficits in a coagulopathic cirrhotic with a recent fall is a strong indicator of concurrent structural pathology.
Do not perform LP before CT head has excluded and neurosurgery has cleared the intracranial mass effect from the SDH — LP in the setting of mass effect and midline shift risks herniation.
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for agitation or sedating opioids for headache — both precipitate and prolong HE in cirrhosis.
Do not initiate anticoagulation or antiplatelet agents without neurosurgical clearance — the SDH with coagulopathy is at risk for expansion.
Do not anchor on ammonia 74 as confirmation of pure HE — ammonia elevation supports HE but does not exclude a concurrent structural lesion.
required_recommendations: Obtain non-contrast CT head urgently — focal right-sided signs (pronator drift, asymmetric hyperreflexia) and unilateral headache in a coagulopathic cirrhotic mandate imaging to exclude structural intracranial pathology; do not defer imaging based on partial lactulose response.

Neurosurgery evaluation of the chronic left-convexity SDH — the right pronator drift and right arm hyperreflexia are contralateral to the left SDH, consistent with mass effect; establish serial CT monitoring schedule and surgical threshold.
Treat the UTI precipitant — urine culture-directed antibiotic therapy; nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (no allergy documented) first-line per susceptibilities.
Correct coagulopathy: target INR <1.5 and platelets >100 x10^9/L before any invasive neurosurgical intervention; avoid anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents while SDH is present.
Titrate lactulose to 3-4 soft stools per day; continue rifaximin 550 mg BID; correct hypokalemia (3.3 mEq/L) and hypomagnesemia — both are HE precipitants via renal ammoniogenesis.

Avoid benzodiazepines and sedating opioids — both worsen HE and are contraindicated; use acetaminophen (hepatic-safe dosing ≤2 g/day) for headache analgesia only after SDH stability confirmed by neurosurgery.

FDG PET has no role in this workup; metabolic encephalopathy and structural SDH have been identified and do not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14), precipitated by urinary tract infection — with concurrent chronic left-convexity subdural hematoma (9 mm, 3 mm rightward midline shift) from cirrhotic coagulopathy and minor fall, identified by mandatory neuroimaging prompted by focal right-sided signs and incomplete lactulose response.

differential.diagnosis: Chronic subdural hematoma as primary cause of AMS (with HE as secondary contributor)
differential.key_features: Left-convexity chronic SDH with right pronator drift and right-arm hyperreflexia — contralateral focal signs mandate neuroimaging and neurosurgical evaluation; coagulopathy + recent fall provide clear mechanism.

differential.diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy alone (pure HE without structural lesion)
differential.key_features: UTI precipitant + elevated ammonia + asterixis supports HE; partial lactulose improvement could be attributed to HE resolution alone if focal signs are missed or attributed to asterixis.

differential.diagnosis: Septic encephalopathy from urinary source (as primary diagnosis rather than HE precipitant)
differential.key_features: Pyuria, nitrites, leukocytosis — UTI is present; in cirrhosis, infection preferentially precipitates HE rather than causing a distinct septic encephalopathy.

Ascites present; absence of peritoneal tenderness and urinalysis strongly positive make UTI the primary infectious source; paracentesis could be performed to exclude if ascites is clinically significant.

differential.diagnosis: Ischemic stroke (left MCA territory given right-sided signs)
differential.key_features: Right arm pronator drift and hyperreflexia raise possibility of left hemispheric stroke; CT shows SDH rather than infarct; no DWI restriction on MRI fallback; focal signs explained by left SDH mass effect.
Fluctuating consciousness in a cirrhotic warrants EEG consideration; no epileptiform activity on EEG (fallback); triphasic-like waves support metabolic rather than epileptic etiology.

key_clinical_evidence: Focal neurological signs (right pronator drift, asymmetric right-arm hyperreflexia, unilateral headache) are NOT features of typical HE and mandate urgent neuroimaging regardless of any ammonia elevation or lactulose response — this is the pack's required 'exclude alternate structural cause with imaging' step.

The laterality is internally consistent: the chronic SDH is on the LEFT convexity, producing a right-sided motor deficit via contralateral mass effect — a known mechanism of chronic SDH presentation that differs from typical bilateral HE.

Partial lactulose response is a known red herring in this scenario — HE can co-exist with and partially improve alongside a concurrent structural lesion; partial improvement should increase, not decrease, the index of suspicion for an additional cause.

Cirrhotic coagulopathy (INR 1.8, platelets 98, low fibrinogen) combined with an unwitnessed minor fall provides the mechanism for the chronic SDH — this is explicitly listed in the HE-ENC criteria pack as an intracranial bleed risk requiring imaging exclusion.

The UTI is the primary HE precipitant (pyuria, nitrites positive, leukocytosis, fever), not the SDH itself — both require simultaneous treatment: antibiotics for the precipitant, neurosurgical management for the structural lesion.

Do not mark CT head or LP as harmful in this case — CT is required per AASLD guidelines; LP is not contraindicated in principle but must be sequenced after CT clears mass effect (the SDH with midline shift is an imaging-before-LP hard constraint).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Partial improvement is consistent with HE responding to lactulose, but the persistent focal right-sided signs and incomplete recovery to GCS 15 mandate neuroimaging — both diagnoses (HE and SDH) can co-exist and must be addressed independently.
red_herrings.data_point: Partial improvement in GCS from 13 to 14 after 24 hours of lactulose escalation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Interpret partial lactulose response as evidence of resolving HE and discontinue further structural workup, missing the concurrent chronic SDH.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ammonia elevation supports HE (per AASLD, it is supportive but not diagnostic and correlates poorly with grade); it does not exclude a concurrent structural lesion. Focal signs mandate CT regardless of ammonia level.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all AMS to the elevated ammonia and treat as straightforward HE without imaging, anchoring on biochemical confirmation of HE.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 62-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) and a prior hepatic encephalopathy episode 9 months ago, now on lactulose and rifaximin secondary prophylaxis, brought to the emergency department by her daughter for a 3-day history of worsening confusion, irritability, and difficulty performing routine tasks. Her daughter reports she found her mother disoriented and unable to manage her medications two days ago. The patient complains of a mild right-temporal headache present for 2 days. She denies hematemesis or melena. Her daughter reports she noticed some dysuria 5 days ago but the patient had not sought care. On review of records, she was seen at an urgent care 10 days ago for a fall at home that was unwitnessed — she was assessed and discharged without imaging. She has been adherent to lactulose and rifaximin based on pill counts. Initial assessment including IV lactulose and empiric measures led to partial improvement in mental status (GCS 13 to 14) after 24 hours, but she remained mildly confused, continued to report headache, and a right pronator drift with asymmetric right-arm hyperreflexia was noted on repeat neurological examination — findings that prompted further evaluation.
